qs.q: Which limitation of a singly linked list is solved by using a doubly linked list?

c.x: Inserting a node at the head is inefficient because all existing nodes must be moved
Deleting the tail node is inefficient because its preceding node cannot be found directly
Traversing from the head toward the tail is impossible because nodes have no next references
Accessing the first node is inefficient because the whole list must be scanned first

qs.e: In a singly linked list each node knows only its successor, so removing the tail (or an interior node) requires finding the preceding node by walking from the head. A doubly linked list stores a prev reference in every node, which removes this asymmetry.

qs.q: A doubly linked list uses header and trailer sentinel nodes. Which statement is true when the list is empty?

c.x: The header's next reference points to the trailer, and the trailer's prev reference points to the header
The header and trailer do not exist until the first element is inserted into the list
The header's next reference and the trailer's prev reference are both empty references
The header's next reference points to itself, and the trailer's prev reference points to itself

qs.e: Sentinels always exist: they only mark the two ends of the list and never store user elements. An empty list is simply <mark>header ↔ trailer</mark> with size 0.

qs.q: A doubly linked list with sentinels holds: `header` ↔ `JFK` ↔ `PVD` ↔ `SFO` ↔ `trailer` The element `BWI` is inserted as the new first element (right after the header). After the insertion, which pair gives the prev and next nodes of `BWI`?

c.x: prev: `header`, next: `trailer`
prev: `JFK`, next: `PVD`
prev: `header`, next: `JFK`
prev: `trailer`, next: `JFK`

e: Find the two neighbors of the new node: predecessor = `header`, successor = `JFK` (the old first node).
Create `BWI` with prev = `header` and next = `JFK`.
Update the neighbors: `header`.next = `BWI` and `JFK`.prev = `BWI`.
<mark>New list: header ↔ BWI ↔ JFK ↔ PVD ↔ SFO ↔ trailer (BWI has prev header, next JFK)</mark>

qs.q:
A doubly linked list with sentinels holds:
`header` ↔ `BWI` ↔ `JFK` ↔ `PVD` ↔ `SFO` ↔ `trailer`
The element `PVD` is removed. Which two references must be <u>changed</u> so that its neighbors bypass it?

c.x: next of `BWI` and prev of `JFK`
next of `PVD` and prev of `PVD`
next of `SFO` and prev of `trailer`
next of `JFK` and prev of `SFO`

e: Identify the neighbors of `PVD`: predecessor = `JFK` (its prev) and successor = `SFO` (its next).
Make the predecessor skip the node: `JFK`.next = `SFO`.
Make the successor skip the node: `SFO`.prev = `JFK`.
`header`, `BWI` and `trailer` are untouched, and the size decreases by 1.
<mark>List after removal: header ↔ BWI ↔ JFK ↔ SFO ↔ trailer</mark>

qs.q: A deque is implemented with a doubly linked list that has header and trailer sentinels. Where is the new node placed by insert_last?

c.x: Between the header sentinel and the first real node
After the trailer sentinel, as a new final node
Between the last real node and the trailer sentinel
Between the first and the second real nodes

qs.e: insert_last inserts between the node just before the trailer and the trailer itself, so no traversal is needed. insert_first mirrors this by inserting right after the header.

qs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a priority queue from an ordinary FIFO queue?

c.x: A priority queue removes the item with the minimum key, regardless of insertion order
A priority queue removes the item that was inserted last, regardless of its key
A priority queue removes the item with the maximum key, regardless of insertion order
A priority queue rejects new insertions after the first removal has taken place

qs.e: A FIFO queue serves the oldest element first. A priority queue serves the element with first priority, i.e., the minimum key, no matter when it was added (key 1 is served before key 2).

qs.q:
An initially empty priority queue `P` receives: `P.add(5,A)`, `P.add(9,C)`, `P.add(3,B)`, `P.add(7,D)`.
What does `P.min()` return, and what happens to that item?

c.x: Returns `(3,B)`; the item is removed from `P`
Returns `(3,B)`; the item stays in `P`
Returns `(5,A)`; the item stays in `P`
Returns `(9,C)`; the item is removed from `P`

e: Order the items by key: `(3,B)`, `(5,A)`, `(7,D)`, `(9,C)`.
`min()` returns the (key, value) tuple with the minimum key, which is `(3,B)`.
`min()` does <u>not</u> remove the item, so `P` is unchanged (unlike `remove_min()`).
<mark>Returns (3,B) and the item stays in P</mark>

qs.q: An empty priority queue `P` receives: `P.add(5,A)`, `P.add(9,C)`, `P.add(3,B)`, `P.add(7,D)`. Then `P.remove_min()` is called four times. Which sequence of tuples is returned?
e: `remove_min()` always removes the item with the <u>minimum</u> key, not the first inserted one.
The keys in the queue are 3, 5, 7, 9.
The four calls therefore return `(3,B)`, then `(5,A)`, then `(7,D)`, then `(9,C)`.
<mark>Sequence: (3,B), (5,A), (7,D), (9,C)</mark>

qs.q: An empty priority queue `P` receives: `P.add(5,A)`, `P.add(9,C)`, `P.add(3,B)`, `P.add(7,D)`. Then `P.remove_min()` is called twice. What do `len(P)` and the next `P.min()` return?
e: Items sorted by key: `(3,B)`, `(5,A)`, `(7,D)`, `(9,C)`.
The first `remove_min()` returns `(3,B)`; the second returns `(5,A)`.
Remaining items: `(7,D)` and `(9,C)`, so `len(P)` is 2.
`min()` returns the smallest remaining key without removing it: `(7,D)`.
<mark>len(P) = 2 and P.min() = (7,D)</mark>

qs.q: All items of a priority queue `P` have been removed with `remove_min()`, so `P` is now empty. What do `P.is_empty()` and one more `P.remove_min()` give?

c.x: `False`, and an error
`True`, and `None`
`True`, and an error
`False`, and `None`

qs.e: Once the last item is removed the queue is empty, so is_empty() returns True. Calling remove_min() on an empty priority queue is not allowed and gives an error.

qs.q: A priority queue of size n is implemented with an unsorted doubly linked list. Which pair of operations takes O(n) worst-case time?

c.x: `add` and `min`
`add` and `remove_min`
`len` and `is_empty`
`min` and `remove_min`

qs.e: add just appends the new item at the end of the list in O(1). But min and remove_min must inspect all entries to find the minimum key, so both take O(n).

qs.q: A priority queue of size n is implemented with a list kept sorted by nondecreasing keys (a doubly linked list). Which operation takes O(n) worst-case time?

c.x: `min`
`remove_min`
`add`
`is_empty`

qs.e: The smallest key is always at the front, so min and remove_min take O(1). But add must scan the list to find the correct position for the new item, which takes O(n) in the worst case.

qs.q: An application performs n add operations and then a single remove_min. Using the worst-case costs of the two list-based priority queues, which implementation is better and why?

c.x: Sorted list: remove_min costs O(1), which outweighs the cost of the adds
Both are equal: each implementation has exactly one O(n) operation
Unsorted list: each add costs O(n) and remove_min costs O(1), so O(n²) total
Unsorted list: n adds cost O(1) each and one remove_min costs O(n), so O(n) total

e: Unsorted list: `add` is O(1) and `remove_min` is O(n).
Cost of the workload: $n \times O(1) + O(n) = O(n)$.
Sorted list: `add` is O(n) (scan for the position) and `remove_min` is O(1).
Cost of the workload: $n \times O(n) + O(1) = O(n^2)$.
<mark>The unsorted list is better: O(n) total instead of O(n²)</mark>

qs.q: A binary heap is a binary tree that satisfies which two properties?

c.x: Heap-order property and full binary tree property
Heap-order property and complete binary tree property
Search-order property and complete binary tree property
Heap-order property and perfect binary tree property

qs.e: A heap needs the heap-order property (for a min-heap, every key is at least as large as its parent's key) and the complete binary tree property (all levels full except possibly the last, which is filled from the left). It is not required to be full or perfect.

qs.q: In a min-heap, which statement is true for every position p other than the root?

c.x: The key at `p` is greater than the keys of both of its children
The key at `p` is less than or equal to the key at its parent
The key at `p` is less than the key at its sibling
The key at `p` is greater than or equal to the key at its parent

qs.e: The heap-order property of a min-heap is $k_p \ge k_{parent}$. Keys never decrease going downward, so the <mark>minimum key is always at the root</mark>. Nothing is required between siblings.

qs.q: A heap stores 10 entries. How many entries are on its last level (level 3, with the root at level 0)?
e: A heap is a complete tree: level $i$ holds $2^i$ nodes for every level except possibly the last.
Levels 0, 1, 2 are full: $1 + 2 + 4 = 7$ entries.
Remaining entries: $10 - 7 = 3$.
<mark>3 entries sit on level 3, in the leftmost positions</mark>

qs.q: A heap stores n = 20 entries. What is its height (counted in edges, root at level 0)?
e: A heap with n entries has height $h = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$.
$\log_2 20 \approx 4.32$.
Taking the floor gives 4.
Check: levels 0 to 3 hold $1+2+4+8 = 15$ entries, so the other 5 entries go on level 4.
<mark>Height = 4</mark>

qs.q: A min-heap (keys only) with 13 entries is given as parent → left child, right child: `4` → `5`, `6` `5` → `15`, `9` `6` → `7`, `20` `15` → `16`, `25` `9` → `14`, `12` `7` → `11`, `13` All other nodes are leaves. A new entry with key `2` is added. Where is the new node first placed (before any swap)?

c.x: As the left child of `16`
As the right child of `13`
As the right child of `20`
As the left child of `20`

e: To keep the tree complete, the new node goes just beyond the rightmost node of the bottom level.
Level 3 already holds `16`, `25`, `14`, `12`, `11`, `13` (the children of `15`, `9`, `7`).
The next free position belongs to `20`, and the leftmost one is its left child.
<mark>The new node is the left child of 20</mark>

qs.q: A min-heap (keys only) with 13 entries is given as parent → left child, right child: `4` → `5`, `6` `5` → `15`, `9` `6` → `7`, `20` `15` → `16`, `25` `9` → `14`, `12` `7` → `11`, `13` All other nodes are leaves. A new entry with key `2` is added and up-heap bubbling is performed. How many swaps occur?
e: The new node `2` is placed as the left child of `20`.
`2` is smaller than its parent `20`, so swap (swap 1).
`2` is smaller than its new parent `6`, so swap (swap 2).
`2` is smaller than its new parent `4` (the root), so swap (swap 3). Now `2` is the root and the process stops.
<mark>3 swaps (equal to the height of the heap)</mark>

qs.q: A min-heap (keys only) with 13 entries is given as parent → left child, right child: `4` → `5`, `6` `5` → `15`, `9` `6` → `7`, `20` `15` → `16`, `25` `9` → `14`, `12` `7` → `11`, `13` All other nodes are leaves. A new entry with key `2` is added and up-heap bubbling finishes. Which keys are the left and right children of the root?

c.x: left child `5`, right child `4`
left child `4`, right child `5`
left child `5`, right child `6`
left child `4`, right child `6`

e: Insert `2` as the left child of `20`.
Swap with `20`: `2` is now the right child of `6`, and `20` is its left child.
Swap with `6`: `2` is now the right child of `4`, and `6` moves down.
Swap with `4`: `2` becomes the root, and `4` takes the right-child position.
The left child `5` was never touched.
<mark>Root 2 has left child 5 and right child 4</mark>

qs.q: Consider this min-heap (keys only) given as parent → left child, right child: `3` → `8`, `5` `8` → `12`, `10` `5` → `9` (left child only) All other nodes are leaves. The key `4` is inserted and up-heap bubbling is performed. What are the children of the node holding `4` in the final heap?

c.x: left child `5`, right child `9`
left child `12`, right child `10`
left child `9`, right child `5`
left child `9`, right child `3`

e: The heap has 6 entries, so the new node takes the next free position: the right child of `5`.
Compare `4` with its parent `5`: `4` is smaller, so swap. Now `4` sits where `5` was, and `5` becomes its right child.
Compare `4` with its new parent `3`: `4` is not smaller, so stop.
<mark>The node 4 has left child 9 and right child 5</mark>

qs.q: In a heap-based priority queue, why is the item at the last position copied to the root during remove_min, instead of simply deleting the root node?

c.x: The last item always holds the second-smallest key, so it is the correct new root
Removing the root would leave two disconnected subtrees, while removing the last leaf keeps the tree complete
The last item is always smaller than both children of the root, so no swaps are needed afterwards
The last item must be removed first so that the heap-order property is never violated

qs.e: The minimum key is stored at the root, and deleting the root directly would split the tree into two subtrees. Deleting the last leaf keeps the tree complete, and its item is copied to the root; down-heap bubbling then restores the heap-order property.

qs.q: A min-heap (keys only) with 13 entries is given as parent → left child, right child: `4` → `5`, `6` `5` → `15`, `9` `6` → `7`, `20` `15` → `16`, `25` `9` → `14`, `12` `7` → `11`, `13` All other nodes are leaves. `remove_min` is performed. Which key is copied to the root in the first step (before down-heap bubbling)?
qs.e: The item at the last position (the rightmost node at the bottom level) replaces the removed root. Here the bottom level ends with `13`, the right child of `7`, so 13 is copied to the root and that leaf is deleted.

qs.q: A min-heap (keys only) with 13 entries is given as parent → left child, right child: `4` → `5`, `6` `5` → `15`, `9` `6` → `7`, `20` `15` → `16`, `25` `9` → `14`, `12` `7` → `11`, `13` All other nodes are leaves. `remove_min` is performed. How many swaps does down-heap bubbling make, and with which keys (in order)?

c.x: 3 swaps: with `5`, then `15`, then `16`
3 swaps: with `5`, then `9`, then `12`
2 swaps: with `5`, then `9`
3 swaps: with `6`, then `7`, then `11`

e: Remove the root `4`, copy the last item `13` to the root, and delete the last leaf (12 entries remain).
`13` has children `5` and `6`. The <u>smaller</u> child is `5`, and `13` is larger, so swap (swap 1).
`13` now has children `15` and `9`. The smaller child is `9`, so swap (swap 2).
`13` now has children `14` and `12`. The smaller child is `12`, so swap (swap 3).
`13` now has no children, so the process stops.
<mark>3 swaps: with 5, then 9, then 12</mark>

qs.q: A min-heap (keys only) with 13 entries is given as parent → left child, right child: `4` → `5`, `6` `5` → `15`, `9` `6` → `7`, `20` `15` → `16`, `25` `9` → `14`, `12` `7` → `11`, `13` All other nodes are leaves. `remove_min` is performed and down-heap bubbling finishes. In the final heap, which keys are the left and right children of the root?

c.x: left child `6`, right child `9`
left child `13`, right child `6`
left child `9`, right child `6`
left child `9`, right child `7`

e: Copy the last item `13` to the root and delete the last leaf.
Down-heap: `13` swaps with the smaller child `5`, so `5` becomes the root.
`13` then swaps with `9` (smaller than `15`), so `9` becomes the left child of the root, and then with `12`.
The right child `6` of the root is never touched.
<mark>Final root 5 with left child 9 and right child 6</mark>

qs.q: A min-heap (keys only) has just had the last item `10` copied to its root during `remove_min`. It is given as parent → left child, right child: `10` → `4`, `5` `4` → `6`, `8` All other nodes are leaves. After down-heap bubbling, which node is the parent of `10`?
e: Root `10` has children `4` and `5`. The smaller child is `4`, so swap: `4` becomes the root.
`10` is now the left child of `4`, with children `6` and `8`. The smaller child is `6`, and `10` is larger, so swap again.
`10` is now a leaf, so the process stops.
<mark>The parent of 10 is 6</mark>

qs.q: A heap is stored in an array (index 0 is the root): `[110, 98, 85, 58, 17, 27, 78, 12, 34]` Which element is the left child of `98`?
e: `98` is stored at index 1.
$\text{leftChildIndex} = 2 \times 1 + 1 = 3$.
<mark>Index 3 holds 58</mark>

qs.q: A heap is stored in an array (index 0 is the root): `[110, 98, 85, 58, 17, 27, 78, 12, 34]` Which element is the parent of `78`?
e: `78` is stored at index 6.
$\text{parentIndex} = \lfloor (6 - 1)/2 \rfloor = \lfloor 2.5 \rfloor = 2$.
<mark>Index 2 holds 85</mark>

qs.q: In an array-based heap (index 0 is the root), a node is stored at index `4`. At which indexes are its left and right children?
e: With index 0 as the root, $\text{leftChildIndex} = 2 \times \text{parentIndex} + 1$.
$\text{rightChildIndex} = 2 \times \text{parentIndex} + 2$.
For parent index 4: left $= 2 \times 4 + 1 = 9$ and right $= 2 \times 4 + 2 = 10$.
<mark>The children are at indexes 9 and 10</mark>

qs.q: Which row gives the running times of a priority queue implemented with a binary heap?

c.x: add O(log n), remove_min O(log n), min O(log n)
add O(log n), remove_min O(log n), min O(1)
add O(1), remove_min O(n), min O(n)
add O(n), remove_min O(1), min O(1)

qs.e: In a heap, add and remove_min only swap along one root-to-leaf path (at most the height, about log n), and min just reads the root in O(1). (For an array-based heap add and remove_min are amortized because of occasional resizing.) Row 3 is the unsorted list and row 4 is the sorted list.

qs.q: In a heap-based priority queue, the worst-case number of swaps performed by add (up-heap bubbling) is bounded by what?

c.x: The number of leaves of the heap
The total number of entries n
The height of the heap, about log n
A constant that does not depend on n

qs.e: The new entry can move up at most one level per swap, from the bottom level to the root, so the number of swaps is at most the height of the heap, $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$. This is why add runs in O(log n).

qs.q: A heap with 12 entries is stored in an array (index 0 is the root). At which index is the last position?
qs.e: Indexes start at 0, so a heap of n entries occupies indexes 0 to n - 1. The last position is at index $n - 1 = 12 - 1 = $ <mark>11</mark>.

qs.q: During down-heap bubbling in a min-heap, the current node p has a left child but no right child. Which child is compared with p?

c.x: Neither child, because the process stops immediately
The parent of p, because the swap goes upward
The sibling of p, because it has the smaller key
The left child, because it is the only child of p

qs.e: If p has no right child, the child c to compare is simply the left child. If p has both children, c is the child with the smaller key. p is swapped with c when p's key is larger than c's key.

qs.q: In the priority queue operation `P.add(k, v)`, what does the key `k` determine?

c.x: The position of the item in insertion order, which fixes its removal turn
The value stored with the item, which is returned by `len(P)`
The priority of the item: the item with the minimum key is removed first
The maximum number of items that `P` is allowed to hold

qs.e: The user designates the priority of an element through its key. The element with the minimum key is the next one removed (key 1 has priority over key 2), while `v` is just the associated value.

qs.q: Why is an array especially suitable for storing a heap?

c.x: A heap is a complete tree, so nodes fill the array without gaps and relatives are found by index arithmetic
A heap is a sorted structure, so its array stays in order and remove_min never needs any swaps
A heap is a full tree, so each node has either zero or two children and parent links are unnecessary
A heap needs random access, so a linked structure would make the heap-order property impossible

qs.e: A complete binary tree has no gaps, so its nodes map to consecutive array indexes level by level. Children and parents are then computed with formulas (such as $2j + 1$ and $\lfloor (j-1)/2 \rfloor$) with no pointers needed.
